t: Who Else But Us
q: It's profoundly misguided for me to assume that I can make claims about what is and isn't valued in a student's home. I've been doing this long enough to have many, many students and families surprise me by revealing things, months or years into knowing them.
Basically, folks are complex; homes and families, even more so. We're better off with a humbler, "I know less than I think" kind of stance toward our students' homes.

There is no one else in the lives of my students more responsible for cultivating Value for learning in my subject area, during the year that my students are with me, than I am. No one is more responsible. No one is better equipped.
This doesn't mean it's our fault if students don't come to value learning while they're with us. It just means that it's our fault if we don't relentlessly aim to bring this increase in Value about.

But regardless of what happens at home, the good news is that the realm I control is powerful. In my classroom — and in yours — there can be grown the kind of life-giving counter-culture where learning is good because it's good.

t: Giving the Proverbial Kick-in-the-Pants Pep Talk
q: Every once in a great while, an unmotivated team member requires a swift kick in the backside to reenergize their focus.

t: The Behavior Illusion Of The First Weeks Of School
q: After the first two or three weeks of school you may be lulled into thinking that you have a great class.

Well, early in the school year students are on their best behavior. They’re attentive and excited. They’re eager and appreciative after a long, boring summer. Many are also trying to turn over a new leaf .
In this day and age, you’re never going to have a great class all on its own. Left to their own devices, your classroom will become Lord of the Flies. Just the way it is.

One day, however, it will catch up to you. The air will feel different. Subtle at first, perhaps, but it’s there. Hints of tension and excitability. Voices on edge. Tinges of disrespect, entitlement, and a slow but sure takeover of your classroom.

All those early halcyon days – if you’re lucky enough to even have them – are no more than an opportunity to set your classroom management plan and its sharply defined rules and consequences in stone.

t: Spin the Dominant Voice
q: A dominant voice during a team discussion often inhibits others from making a contribution

The maneuver employed by master facilitators is to redirect the dominant party’s contribution toward the group.
Taking something said and redirecting it allows others to take the floor.
Good leaders simply can’t allow any voice to overwhelm team discussion or drown out other voices.

t: Should You Tell Students You Like Them
q: I'm talking about things like this: "Oh, Mr. Stuart? Yeah, he doesn't like me. I talk too much in his class.

The trick with the Five Key Beliefs approach to student motivation is that you can't force students to believe things. All you can do is get really intentional about the signals you're transmitting to them.

Even if you're the most intentional teacher in the world about the signals you're sending to your students, you still don't know if some of your signals might be getting received as "I DON'T LIKE YOU, PUNY STUDENT!!!
And that's why it's so helpful to say sometimes, in a way that makes sense coming from you, things like this: Hey, just so you know — I like you. I think you're great.
And as you're doing it, picture yourself practicing a skill, like an athlete practices a sport. You're gaining muscle. You're building strength.

t: How to Have Fun Helping Your Students Value School This Year
q: When students don't optimally Value school, they'll say things like this: This is boring. This is pointless. Why do we have to do this?

Here's why: your classroom is an alternate world from the one your students normally inhabit. Or at least, it should be. It's a cosmos — Latinized from the Greek kosmos: a good order, an orderly arrangement; a world.

Whether you teach art or agriculture, social studies or Scripture, English language arts or personal finance, you are, day by day, through helping your students toward mastery of your discipline, inviting them in to a cosmos.

When your students respond to your high-impact lessons with moans and groans, this need not frighten or bother you. There's a way to become so sure of the goodness of what you have on offer in your cosmos that you don't bat an eye when folks are genuinely hesitant about its goodness.

t: A Critical Mistake Teachers Make On The First Day Of School https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2022/08/05/mistake-teachers-make-the-first-day-of-school/
q: You see, there is a mistake teachers make during the window of time between teaching their plan and enforcing their plan.
But here’s the thing: You just got finished emphatically teaching your rules and consequences and explaining their supreme importance. You just promised to follow through no matter what.

But it’s a critical mistake. No matter how unpleasant it may seem at the time, if a student breaks a rule, you must enforce . There is no window of time. No grace period. No kinda-sorta easing into it.
The second you finish teaching your classroom management plan you must go live. You must send the message that you mean what you say. If a student misbehaves right away, you should celebrate.
When you don’t follow through you communicate to your new students that you’re a pushover who can’t be trusted, doesn’t mean what they say, and isn’t serious about classroom management.
